subject: Meaning of coefficients from allometry analysis

messages.author: e358c6bea2b9961c
messages.subject: Meaning of coefficients from allometry analysis
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm trying to understand what exactly the coefficients obtanined by doing a procD.lm analysis mean.

Using the plethodon example and running the example model fit.full (coords ~ log(Csize) + species * site),  fit.full$coefficients is an array with 5 rows and 24 columns. The columns are clearly landmark coordinates, and the rows are expected terms in a regression analysis:
 "(Intercept)"           "log(Csize)"            "speciesTeyah"          "siteSymp"   "speciesTeyah:siteSymp"

My question is: what are these 5 shapes and what they represent? Are they extreme shapes for each site and species?
Also, why are they 5? If  "(Intercept)"  stands for siteAllo for example and "log(Csize)"  for speciesTeyah:siteAllo (based on how a standard lm regression in R works), where are the shapes for speciesJord?

I add the code at the end so it's easier to reproduce this example.
Thanks a lot, best wishes
Agnese

-----------------------------
library(geomorph)
data("plethodon")

Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)    #GPA-alignment

fit.full <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + species * site, data = gdf,
iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE, turbo = TRUE) #allometry model

fit.full$coefficients
dimnames(fit.full$coefficients)
head(fit.full$coefficients)

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Meaning of coefficients from allometry analysis
parts:
Dear Agnese,

Hear is the textbook definition.  Coefficients are scalars that express the expected per unit changes in a set of dependent or response variables, based on the parameters of a linear model design matrix.  In this case there are 24 dependent variables (Procrustes residuals) and 5 parameters required for the three independent variables and the interaction between two of them.  I suspect that your question does not seek the textbook definition as much as it seeks the understanding you might attain from thorough reading of a linear models textbook.  There is no way to overcome that in a few sentences.  In my opinion, working with geometric morphometrics requires some training in linear models.  Virtually all analyses in geometric morphometrics, or in statistics for that matter, are based on linear models.  (Most introductory statistics courses do not include a teaching of linear models, which is unfortunate, in my opinion.)  I suspect that any formal training in geometric morphometrics also includes training in linear models.  (Any workshop for which I have been involved as participant or instructor has.)  If the terms “linear model design matrix” or “coefficients” do not have clear meaning, it probably means one’s training in linear models is limited, and I recommend remedying that more than attempting to understand geometric morphometrics without this training.

In terms of coefficient labels in R, they match linear model design matrix parameters (columns), which includes an intercept.  One can deduce that the intercept corresponds to estimation of shapes for allopatric Plethodon jordani, because “speciesTayah" means the expected amount of shape change if a species in Plethodon teyahalee and “siteSymp” means the expected amount of shape change if the specimen is from a sympatric site.  The first part of each term (e.g., species) is the variable name and the second part is the level of variable being changed (e.g., Teyah”).  By process of elimination, neither Jord nor Allo are listed as coefficients, so these must be the starting conditions (the intercept).  Again, if this explanation does not seem to make much sense, it probably means a limited understanding of linear model designs rather than R’s way of identifying coefficients.

Here is a good linear models source:

Rencher, A. C., & Schaalje, G. B. (2008). Linear models in statistics. John Wiley & Sons.

I believe there are pirated copies on the internet.

hope this helps.

Mike

Dear Agnese,

I am also having issues with Google groups (not just geomorph) including messages appearing in my inbox and then disappearing.  I went to the main google group page to retrieve your response and I post it here in case it did not register for others (like me), with some annotations below.

Hi Mike,

I can't seem to reply on the previous thread.

Thanks for your answer. I know understand the 5 terms provided in fit.full$coefficients. I got an explanation of linear models in a basic R course, so it is sometimes hard to relate those basic concepts to models created by complex GM matrices.

As now I have a better understanding of what I'm looking at and assuming procD.lm coefficients are overall similar to the coefficients obtained by doing a standard lm() linear model, 

Actually, they should be exactly the same.  procD.lm is a wrapper for lm.rrpp, making it possible to use coordinate data in a (3D) array as data (whereas lm.rrpp requires a matrix).  The lm.rrpp function is the same as lm, only it performs the lm analysis many times, each time randomizing residuals.  The observed case provides the same coefficients, fitted values, residuals, etc.

do I need to add the deltas of each coordinate for each taxon to the taxon of reference in the dataset in order to be able to extract the shapes representing the slopes for each species?

I’m not sure I fully understood, but it sounds like you wish to do one of two different things.  One, is estimate shapes.  This can be done really easily with the predict.lm.rrpp function (there is an example showing how), and plots with confidence ellipses can be made.  Alternatively, maybe you want to isolate, e.g., the effect of changing the mean shape coefficient by coefficient?  This is a little trickier.  You would have to first create your own design matrices (vectors, really) and multiply them times the coefficients.  Here is an example, using the procD.lm example.

> data(plethodon) 
> Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land, print.progress = FALSE)   
> gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, 
+                            site = plethodon$site, 
+                            species = plethodon$species) # geomorph data frame
> 
> fit1 <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + species * site, 
+                  data = gdf, iter = 999, turbo = TRUE,
+                  RRPP = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)
> 
> X <- model.matrix(fit1)
> x <- colMeans(X) # a vector of the means of parameters
> B <- coef(fit1)
> 
> Mean <- x %*% B # should be vector of mean shape
> Mean

[1,] 0.06151527 0.5492549 -0.06921856
> 
> # compare
> Y.gpa$consensus
             X            Y

> 
> # same !
> 
> # just the effect of centroid size (common allometry)
> 
> xc <- x
> xc[3:5] <- 0
> xc # zero out non-targetted coefficients
          (Intercept)            log(Csize)          speciesTeyah

          (Intercept)            log(Csize)          speciesTeyah

I'm trying to plot these slope shapes on a phylomorphospace. My dataset has ontogentic series for the taxa and mutiple specimens, therefore a standard phylomorphospace is not an option.

No but you can get coefficients from a PGLS fit and plot predicted values or effects of coefficients like above.
